course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Global Conflict
unit.description: Study how empires collapsed, why two world wars were fought and how they were conducted, how the Depression reshaped economies, and how mass atrocities happened.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.7 key concept: World War II was a total war in which governments mobilized economies, populations, and propaganda, and new technology increased civilian casualties
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing total war in 1939–1945
stimulusBlocks.text:
World War II was fought by entire societies. The United States converted car factories to build tanks and planes, and millions of women took industrial jobs. The Soviet Union moved whole factories east, beyond the reach of German armies. Governments rationed food and fuel and used films and posters to build support.

Civilians were targets as never before. Bombing destroyed cities in Britain, Germany, the Soviet Union, China, and Japan. The war killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, more than half of them civilians, including about 27 million Soviet citizens.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, about how many Soviet citizens died in the war?
choices: About 27 million
About 2.7 million
About 270,000
About 70 million
choiceExplanations: The passage says about 27 million.
The figure is ten times higher.
The figure is far higher.
That is the total for the whole war.
questions.distinguisher: 70 to 85 million is the estimate for all deaths in the war.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.7 key concept: technological advances, including the atomic bomb, changed the conduct and outcome of World War II
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the decision to use the atomic bomb, 1945
stimulusBlocks.text:
In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing more than 100,000 people immediately and many more from injuries and radiation afterward. Japan surrendered days later.

Historians still debate the decision. Some argue that the bombs ended the war without an invasion that would have cost many lives on both sides. Others argue that Japan was near surrender or that US leaders also wanted to show the Soviet Union the power of the new weapon.

proving that the bombs were the only option
questions.explanation: It sets out several historians' arguments.
choiceExplanations: It discusses the decision, not design.
It sets out several historians' arguments.
It presents a debate.
It does not settle the question for either side.
questions.distinguisher: The passage presents both sides without proving one.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is shown by the examples in the passage?
choices: Governments ended rationing to raise morale
Civilians were kept away from the fighting
Governments redirected industry and labor to war production
Industry stayed in private hands with little state direction
questions.explanation: The United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain all shifted factories and workers to military needs.
choiceExplanations: The passage says Britain rationed food and fuel.
The passage says civilians were bombed and became targets.
The United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain all shifted factories and workers to military needs.
The examples show governments directing factories and labor, not leaving them alone.
questions.distinguisher: American industry stayed privately owned, but the government directed what it made, so the state was far from hands-off.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 7.7 key concept: governments mobilized economies and civilians for total war in World War II
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing economic mobilization and bombing in World War II, 1939–1945
stimulusBlocks.text:
During World War II, governments mobilized entire economies. In the United States, factories that had made cars built tanks and aircraft, and millions of women took jobs in war industries. In the Soviet Union, Stalin ordered factories moved east of the Ural Mountains ahead of the German advance, and they produced weapons in huge numbers that helped the Red Army turn back the invasion. Britain rationed food and fuel and drafted women into war work and the armed forces.

Civilians became targets as well. German bombing of London and Coventry and Allied bombing of Dresden and Tokyo killed hundreds of thousands of people.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares Soviet and American wartime economies as described in the passage?
choices: Both relied on factories relocated beyond the Ural Mountains
Both shifted to war production, but the Soviet state relocated whole industries
Only the Soviet Union employed women in war industries
The American government directed production while the Soviet government left it to private firms
questions.explanation: The passage notes Stalin's relocation of factories as a response to the German advance, which the United States did not face.
choiceExplanations: Only the Soviet Union relocated factories in the passage.
The passage notes Stalin's relocation of factories as a response to the German advance, which the United States did not face.
The passage says millions of American women worked in war industries.
The Soviet state owned its industries and directed them, so the contrast is false.
questions.distinguisher: Both economies used women's labor, but only the Soviet Union had to move factories away from an invading army.

questions.prompt: The bombing of cities by both sides illustrates which feature of World War II?
choices: Trench warfare along fixed fronts of the kind seen in 1914
Nonviolent resistance to occupation by foreign armies
Wars of national unification like those of the 1800s
Total war, with civilians and factories as targets
questions.explanation: Bombing of London, Coventry, Dresden, and Tokyo aimed at civilian morale and industrial capacity.
choiceExplanations: Trench warfare was typical of World War I and is not shown in the passage.
The passage describes bombing, not nonviolent resistance.
National unification wars belong to the nineteenth century.
Bombing of London, Coventry, Dresden, and Tokyo aimed at civilian morale and industrial capacity.
questions.distinguisher: World War I also mobilized economies for total war, but massive bombing of cities was characteristic of World War II.
